title: The nutrient delivery investigation
subtitle: Cross the gut wall, travel in blood, reach a tissue
objective: Describe how absorbed nutrients and water reach body tissues and distinguish this from the waste route.

sow.exactOutcome: Describe how nutrients and water are transported in the body.
sow.alignment: Directly develops this stated outcome with secondary-age tasks at an upper-KS2 conceptual level. Support and stretch are flexible; this exemplar is not a claim of qualification approval.

priorLearning: Know the jobs of digestion and circulation.
Trace blood through heart, lungs and body.
success: Trace a soluble nutrient or water from intestine into blood and towards tissues.
Distinguish unabsorbed gut material from urine made by kidneys.

vocabulary.meaning: The movement of substances across a surface into the body’s transport systems.
Able to dissolve in a liquid.
A small sugar the body can use in respiration.
The liquid part of blood, mostly water.
An organ that filters blood and helps balance water and dissolved substances.

equipment: Shared route/evidence cards, selected pupil route, pencils, optional paper tokens.
preparation: Explain that a glucose token represents a molecule; it is not a visible crumb.
All transport diagrams are selective models, not exact anatomy or a literal sieve.
safety: No food, liquids, bodily samples or pupil measurements are used.
Do not prescribe how much water a pupil should drink or ask for toilet/medical disclosures.
practicalAlternative: Every pupil can use the supplied paper tokens and route cards. The model needs no practical materials.

misconceptions.claim: Absorption and digestion are the same job.
misconceptions.correction: Digestion breaks some food substances down; absorption moves substances across the gut wall.
misconceptions.check: Ask which job changes food molecules and which moves substances across a surface.

misconceptions.claim: Water goes from stomach directly to bladder.
misconceptions.correction: Water is absorbed into the body; kidneys filter blood and make urine.
misconceptions.check: Ask where the kidneys get the water they remove.

misconceptions.claim: All food enters the bloodstream unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Small absorbable substances cross the gut wall; unabsorbed material continues through the digestive tract.
misconceptions.check: Ask where a whole bread crumb belongs.

access.supported: Use route words and sort tokens with sentence frames.
access.standard: Explain two substance journeys and distinguish waste routes.
access.stretch: Repair a delivery model and explain simplification and uncertainty.
access.regulation: Offer quiet pointing, private writing, drawing or adult scribing. Pass-and-return for public questions. Use fictional cases; no personal medical disclosure or comparison of bodies. Assign response routes from current evidence, not fixed pupil labels.

sources.title: NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Digestion, absorption, transport and water absorption. Paraphrased factual reference; diagrams and activities are original.

sources.title: NIDDK: Your kidneys and how they work
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Kidneys filter blood and regulate water; urine does not come directly from a stomach-to-bladder tube.

sources.title: NHLBI: How blood flows through the heart

slides.title: Two tokens need a route
body: One token is glucose. One is water.
How can both reach a muscle tissue?
slides.notes: These are molecule models, not food crumbs. Invite a predicted route; do not mark guesses publicly.

slides.title: Recover the two system jobs
body: R1. What is digestion?
R2. What does the heart pump?
R3. Where does blood gain oxygen?
slides.notes: R1 breakdown into smaller absorbable substances; R2 blood; R3 lungs. Explain that today focuses on crossing the gut wall, not repeating the full heart route.

slides.title: I separate breaking down from crossing
body: Digestion changes some food substances.
Absorption moves substances across the gut wall.
I follow a small glucose molecule.
slides.notes: Think aloud: A crumb is not the transported token. I choose glucose, a small dissolved molecule. It crosses the intestinal lining into blood. The arrow shows net entry, not an empty hole. Actual absorption involves cells and transport processes; mechanism names are not required.

visual.title: Absorption: across a surface
visual.description: Small glucose symbols cross the intestinal wall into a capillary. Labels distinguish intestine contents, wall and blood. The model is not to scale or a literal sieve.

elements.text: A soluble nutrient crosses the gut wall

Particles and wall are not to scale. This shows absorption,
not a literal hole or a whole-food filter.

slides.title: I follow the transport job
body: Water and many nutrients travel in blood plasma.
Blood moves towards body tissues.
Water can be absorbed without digestion.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Think aloud: Water is already a small substance; I do not need to cut it into smaller food units. Water is absorbed in small and large intestine. Most glucose from gut travels first through liver before wider circulation; detailed organ route omitted in this job map.

visual.description:
A simplified scientific sequence: Intestine:
absorption; Blood plasma:
transport; Body tissues:
substances used. Circulation carries substances onwards. This job map
omits the detailed liver, heart and lung route.

Circulation carries substances onwards. This job map

slides.title: I separate two waste routes
body: Unabsorbed gut material can leave as faeces.
Kidneys filter blood and make urine.
There is no direct gut-to-bladder tube.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace each row separately. The urine row is simplified: ureters carry urine from kidneys to bladder and urethra carries it out. No pupil experiences are requested.

visual.title: Two different routes out
visual.description: A branching model distinguishes unabsorbed material continuing through large intestine to faeces, from blood being filtered by kidneys to produce urine.

elements.text: Faeces and urine take different routes
No direct intestine-to-bladder tube is shown or implied.

slides.title: Delivery desk: assign the tokens
body: W1. Match each token to its next process.
Use cards A–F on page 1.
Explain using “break down”, “cross” or “carry”.
slides.notes: Tokens: large starch molecule needing digestion→break down; glucose at gut wall→absorption; dissolved glucose in blood→transport; water in the gut→absorption. No physical substances are used.

slides.title: The incorrect shortcut
body: Diagram claim: “Drink → stomach → bladder.”
W2. Replace the middle route.
Which organ makes urine from blood?
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Correct core chain: intestine absorption→blood→kidneys make urine→bladder. Do not imply all ingested water immediately becomes urine or use a fixed percentage.

slides.title: Choose the right exit route
body: A food particle remains unabsorbed.
W3. Does it enter blood or continue through the gut?
Explain how this differs from urine.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Unabsorbed material continues through the gut towards faeces; kidneys produce urine by filtering blood. Some gut residues are changed by bacteria, so the model does not claim that all food remains unchanged.
slides.reveal: Unabsorbed material continues through the gut. Kidneys make urine by filtering blood.

slides.title: A water molecule is in the small intestine
body: Which next step can happen?
slides.notes: A is incorrect: water does not need digestion into smaller food molecules. B is correct: water can be absorbed across the gut wall. C is incorrect: there is no direct intestine-to-bladder tube. Revisit the absorption diagram.

options.text: It must be digested before absorption.
options.feedback: Water does not need digestion into smaller food molecules.

options.text: It can be absorbed across the gut wall.
options.feedback: Water is absorbed in the small and large intestine.

options.text: It goes through a direct pipe to the bladder.
options.feedback: Kidneys make urine from blood; there is no direct stomach-to-bladder pipe.

slides.title: Create the delivery explanation
body: Choose one response route.
Explain a glucose journey and a water journey.
Keep the two waste routes separate.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across You do. Support route provides words; standard explains order; stretch repairs ambiguity and includes model limitation.

slides.title: Use three different verbs
body: Digestion: break down.
Absorption: cross a surface.
Transport: carry onwards.
slides.notes: Shared time. A pupil may point to a verb card and dictate an explanation. These verbs distinguish processes rather than competing systems.

slides.title: Check the substance at each arrow
body: Is it whole food or a small molecule?
Is it inside the gut, blood or a tissue?
Have you named the process?
slides.notes: Shared time. Never accept “food goes into blood” without clarifying a small absorbed substance. Water need not be digested.

slides.title: Trace and challenge
body: Trace one partner or teacher model.
Find a clear process label.
Ask for a missing step or clarification.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Offer private check. A diagram with appropriate verbs can demonstrate equivalent understanding to prose.

slides.title: Choose a closer look
body: Would magnifying gut wall or kidney help next?
Explain which unanswered question it would address.
slides.notes: Lundy: teacher records pupil questions, selects one magnified view and explains how pupil reasoning determined the next illustration.

slides.title: Three steps, three meanings
body: E1. What does absorption mean?
E2. What carries many dissolved nutrients?
E3. Which organs make urine from blood?
slides.notes: E1: absorption means crossing a surface into the body’s transport systems. E2: blood or plasma. E3: kidneys. E4 on the pupil page: water does not need digestion before absorption.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: delivery routes
pupilPages.intro: Use these science cards for paper tokens or the interactive model. No measurements from pupils are needed.

cards.title: A • Digestion
cards.text: Some large food molecules are broken into small molecules. Glucose is a small soluble sugar.

cards.title: B • Absorption
cards.text: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. Glucose crosses its wall into blood; most dietary fat initially takes a lymph route.

cards.title: C • Water
cards.text: Water is absorbed in both small and large intestine. It does not need to be digested into a smaller substance.

cards.title: D • Transport
cards.text: Blood plasma is mostly water and carries many dissolved substances. Circulation moves them towards tissues.

cards.title: E • Unabsorbed material
cards.text: Material that is not absorbed continues through the large intestine. Faeces are stored in the rectum and leave through the anus.

cards.title: F • Kidneys
cards.text: Kidneys filter blood and help balance water and dissolved substances. They make urine, which is carried to and stored in the bladder.

blocks.prompt: W1. Choose the process for large starch, glucose at gut wall, glucose in blood and water in gut.
W2. Repair “drink → stomach → bladder”.
W3. Explain the route of unabsorbed material and how urine differs.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: follow the substance
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Word bank: absorption / digestion / transport / blood / kidneys.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which process breaks some large food molecules down?
S2. Complete: Glucose crosses the gut wall by ____ . It is carried in ____ towards tissues.
S3. Does water have to be digested before it is absorbed?
S4. Draw a route for water: intestine → ____ → body tissues. Label the crossing step.
S5. Complete: ____ make urine from blood. Unabsorbed material continues through the ____ . Word bank: gut / kidneys.
S6. Explain one difference between digestion and transport.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: two delivery records
pupilPages.intro: Use precise substance and process names.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the table, then give one example of absorption.
N2. Trace glucose from the small intestine across its wall and towards a body tissue. Label each process.
N3. Trace absorbed water towards tissues. Explain why digestion is not needed for water.
N4. Compare the faeces route with the urine route. Include the kidneys.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: audit the delivery animation
pupilPages.intro: An accurate model states what it shows and what it simplifies.

blocks.prompt: T1. Repair “Whole food travels through blood to muscles”. Use digestion, absorption and transport accurately.
T2. Explain a water journey and why “all swallowed water goes directly to the bladder” is wrong.
T3. A diagram sends every dietary nutrient straight into blood. Use card B to name a limitation and improve its label.
T4. Explain why a gut-wall diagram is not a literal kitchen sieve. State what its arrows represent.
E1. What is absorption?
E2. What transports many dissolved nutrients around the body?
E3. Which organs make urine by filtering blood?
E4. Does water need digestion before absorption? Explain.
Reflection. Which route would you like to magnify and why?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1 breakdown of some food substances into smaller absorbable substances. R2 blood. R3 lungs.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 large starch needing digestion: digestion; glucose at gut wall: absorption; glucose in blood: transport; water in the gut: absorption. W2 water is absorbed from intestine into body transport; blood reaches kidneys which make urine carried to bladder. Not all swallowed water becomes urine. W3 unabsorbed material continues through large intestine to faeces; kidneys make urine from blood.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A incorrect: water does not need digestion. B correct: it can cross the gut wall. C incorrect: kidneys filter blood rather than a direct pipe from stomach.

answers.label: S1–S6
answers.answer: S1 digestion. S2 absorption; blood. S3 no. S4 intestine→blood→tissues, with absorption at gut wall. S5 kidneys; gut. S6 digestion breaks some food substances down; transport carries absorbed substances onwards.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 digestion/breakdown; absorption/crossing surface into body transport; transport/carrying onwards. Glucose or water crossing gut wall is a valid example. N2 glucose crosses small intestine wall into blood and is carried towards tissues. Full correct liver/heart/lung route may be added but not required. N3 water absorbed into blood and distributed; already a small substance, not needing digestion. N4 gut residues→large intestine→rectum/anus/faeces; blood→kidneys→ureters/bladder→urine route. Names beyond kidneys/bladder optional.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 some food molecules are digested into small substances such as glucose, absorbed through the gut wall and transported in blood. T2 absorption precedes distribution; kidneys regulate water by filtering blood; water also remains in the body or leaves by other routes. T3 most dietary fats initially enter lymph rather than directly blood; label “a soluble nutrient such as glucose” instead of every nutrient. T4 gut wall is living tissue with cells and transport processes, not mesh holes; arrows represent substance movement, not whole food crumbs.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: E1 movement across a surface into the body’s transport systems. E2 blood/plasma. E3 kidneys. E4 no; water can be absorbed without breakdown into smaller food units. Reflection: any reasoned magnification question.

answers.label: Assessment and re-teach
answers.answer: Secure: distinguishes three processes, describes glucose/water absorption and blood transport, and separates kidney urine from gut residue. If vocabulary alone is correct, require a substance arrow. If direct-bladder error persists, trace the two parallel waste routes with different tokens.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.

This lesson zooms in on crossing surfaces and transporting substances; the previous heart lesson supplies the detailed circulation route. Diagrams omit the liver, heart and lungs in some job maps and explicitly state that limitation.
Most dietary fat takes a lymphatic route before joining circulation. Core pupils follow glucose; stretch evaluates an “all nutrients directly to blood” claim.
Interactive route predictions map to W1–W3. On paper, move labelled tokens and explain each process aloud or in writing; no literal sieve experiment is proposed.

interactive.title: Delivery desk: predict the next process
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
